lessons.title: Master vs. Reference vs. Transactional Data

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one entity your own organization (or household, if between jobs) tracks in more than one place -- a contact, a product, a vendor. List every system or spreadsheet that has its own copy, and note one field that disagrees between at least two of them. Then open any order, invoice, or transaction record you have access to and sort every field on it into master, reference, or transactional data. Finally, decide which of the four MDM architecture styles (registry, consolidation, coexistence, centralized) is closest to how your chosen entity is actually managed today, or describe the gap if none fit cleanly.
slots.deliverable: A written list of disagreeing systems/fields for one real entity, a field-by-field master/reference/transactional classification of one real transaction record, and a named (or described-gap) architecture style for that entity.

slots.practicalActivity: Draft a one-paragraph MDM business case for your own organization (or a hypothetical one), using only the real cost categories from this lesson -- duplicate outreach, blocked automation, inconsistent reporting, failed integrations -- and one specific, citable example, with no invented statistics. Then draft the skeleton of an MDM policy for the Customer domain: who would own it, which fields matter most, and one match rule you'd want written down rather than left to memory.
slots.deliverable: A one-paragraph, citable MDM business case, plus a skeleton MDM policy for the Customer domain naming an owner, key fields, and one documented match rule.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice: pick a second real or hypothetical domain, different from the previous two slots, and produce a full Chapter 1 analysis for it in one pass -- classify it as master, reference, or transactional, name its closest architecture style, write a one-sentence citable business case, and name who would own its governance -- without referring back to the lesson videos.
slots.deliverable: A one-page Chapter 1 brief for a new domain, covering classification, architecture style, business case, and governance ownership.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a dataset you have access to with at least a few hundred rows of people or organizations (a contact export is fine). Propose one blocking key you'd use before running detailed matching, and justify why it's cheap to compute and unlikely to split a true match across two blocks. Then take two records you believe refer to the same entity but aren't identical, and decide which fields would support a deterministic rule versus which would contribute most to a probabilistic similarity score.
slots.deliverable: A justified blocking-key proposal for one real dataset, plus a deterministic-vs-probabilistic field breakdown for one real near-duplicate pair.

slots.practicalActivity: Think of a system you use (a CRM, a contacts list, a spreadsheet) with a known or suspected duplicate entry. Identify which of the four causes from this lesson most likely created it, and whether a point-of-entry check would have caught it. Then, using a three-system customer example (CRM, billing, shipping each with a slightly different record for the same person), sketch what a golden record for that customer would look like -- which system's phone number and address you'd use, and why.
slots.deliverable: A duplicate-cause diagnosis for one real system, plus a sketched golden record for a 3-system customer example with sourcing decisions justified.

slots.practicalActivity: For the same 3-system customer example, write one survivorship rule per field (phone, address, email), naming the strategy -- most recent wins, trusted source wins, most complete wins, or most frequent wins -- and why. Then, for a hypothetical candidate match pair (same last name, same city, different first name, different phone number), decide whether you'd merge, reject, or flag it as needing more data, and name one additional piece of evidence that would change your mind.
slots.deliverable: A per-field survivorship rule set for the customer example, plus a reasoned merge/reject/needs-more-data call on a sample match pair.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab: run the full matching-and-consolidation pipeline end to end on one real or realistic entity -- propose a blocking key, classify a candidate pair as a deterministic or probabilistic match, resolve one duplicate into a golden record, write its per-field survivorship rules, and make a merge/reject/needs-more-data call on at least one uncertain pair -- all in a single worked example.
slots.deliverable: One complete worked matching-and-consolidation pipeline for a real or realistic entity: blocking key, match classification, golden record, survivorship rules, and a steward decision on one uncertain pair.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a company you've been a customer of that has multiple divisions or subsidiaries. Sketch what you believe its customer hierarchy looks like from your own experience, including where your own account sits and what the ultimate parent is. Then pick a physical product you own that comes in multiple variants (sizes, flavors, colors), identify its product level versus its SKU level, and list 3 attributes that stay the same across every SKU and 3 that differ SKU by SKU.
slots.deliverable: A sketched customer hierarchy for one real company, plus a product-vs-SKU attribute breakdown for one real product with variants.

slots.practicalActivity: If you've ever submitted an invoice or been paid as a contractor, list every piece of information you had to provide before getting paid for the first time, and map each item to a vendor-master attribute from this lesson -- flagging which one would be most dangerous to accept changed without verification. Then, for an employer you know well, list three systems besides HR that need to know when an employee joins or leaves, and note for each whether the update happens automatically from HR or requires manual re-entry.
slots.deliverable: A vendor-onboarding-to-master-attribute mapping with a flagged fraud risk, plus a 3-system employee-sync gap analysis for one real employer.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one hierarchy from the previous two slots (the customer family tree or an employee reporting chain). Sketch it as a simple parent-child table with 3-4 rows -- an ID column and a parent ID column -- and trace by hand how you'd roll a number up from the bottom row to the top.
slots.deliverable: A parent-child table sketch for one real hierarchy, with a hand-traced roll-up calculation from the bottom level to the top.

slots.practicalActivity: List five reference data sets from everyday software you use (status dropdowns, country selectors, category filters). For each, decide whether it's internal or external, and note what would break if the list silently changed overnight. Then pick one status or category dropdown you've seen change over time in a real app, and sketch what likely happened to the old values in its underlying code table -- were old records relabeled, or did the old code just stop being offered for new entries.
slots.deliverable: A 5-item internal/external reference-data classification with break-if-changed notes, plus a sketched code-lifecycle (deprecated vs. deleted) analysis for one real dropdown.

slots.practicalActivity: Argue for centralized reference data governance as the right fit for a mid-sized company with five business units on different core systems, then argue the distributed case in two sentences -- note which argument you found more convincing. Then think of two apps or systems you've used that both track the same kind of status, and sketch a four-row cross-reference table mapping one system's status values to the other's, identifying whether the mapping is one-to-one or many-to-one.
slots.deliverable: A centralized-vs-distributed governance argument with a stated conclusion, plus a 4-row cross-reference table for two real systems with its mapping type identified.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one master data domain from the previous chapter and one change that could happen to it (a customer's credit hold, a product going out of stock, a vendor's bank details changing). Decide whether that change belongs in batch or real-time distribution, and explain the real-world consequence of getting it wrong in either direction. Then pick any list you maintain yourself (contacts, vendors, subscriptions) with at least 20 rows, and score it against completeness, uniqueness, and validity, writing down the three percentages.
slots.deliverable: A batch-vs-real-time distribution decision with consequences for one real domain change, plus a 3-dimension (completeness/uniqueness/validity) quality score for one real personal list.

slots.practicalActivity: Take one real system pairing from your own work or a hobby project where the same fact has to agree across two places. Decide which of the three mechanisms (batch, API, event-driven) actually connects them today, whether that matches how fresh the data needs to be, and what would break first if it stayed mismatched. Then pick two tools named in this lesson (Informatica MDM, Reltio, SAP MDG, Microsoft SQL Server Master Data Services, Profisee) and write one sentence per evaluation criterion -- domain coverage, architecture-style fit, matching engine, integration support, ecosystem fit, cost -- on which would fit better for a company already invested in one ecosystem.
slots.deliverable: An integration-mechanism mismatch analysis for one real system pairing, plus a criterion-by-criterion comparison of two named MDM tools for a stated ecosystem.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one "which number is right" disagreement from your own work, school, or a hobby project. Sketch a mini version of the Brightfield Outdoor Supply fix from this lesson's case study: one matching rule you'd use to find duplicates, one survivorship rule to decide which value wins, and one place you'd keep the single standard list going forward -- walking through how each of this course's five chapters would apply to your scenario, the way Brightfield's chapter-by-chapter walkthrough does.
slots.deliverable: A one-page mini case-study write-up applying all 5 chapters of this course (foundations, matching, domains, reference data, enterprise consistency) to one real or realistic "which number is right" disagreement.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can design a matching and survivorship strategy for a master data domain, build and document a golden record from duplicate source records, and define the reference-data governance and distribution plan that keeps that golden record consistent across every system that consumes it.
